title: One React application, owned by Rust
excerpt: ZapJS keeps the Next.js-style application model while moving the runtime, build graph and deployment artifact ownership into Rust.
paragraphs: ZapJS is built around one application graph. Pages, layouts, route handlers, server actions, client references, browser chunks, static assets and cache metadata are produced from the same model.
Rust owns request admission, route planning, body limits, cancellation and host capabilities. React remains real React JavaScript, executed inside a Rust-controlled engine for server work.
The target deployment is still one managed project output: static assets, browser chunks, server bundles, manifest data and Rust-managed dynamic artifacts produced together.

The current repository contains the Rust foundation crates for routing, Splice, rendering and TSX bundling. The remaining work is connecting those crates into the full React SSR, Flight, hydration, actions and managed deployment vertical slice.
author: ZapJS

title: Splice is an internal Rust boundary
excerpt: Splice exists for process isolation and replacement inside the framework runtime.
paragraphs: Splice version 2 is a bounded Rust-to-Rust transport. It supports unary invocation, typed remote errors, negotiated frame limits, max in-flight admission, deadlines, cancellation and connection-failure cleanup.
That boundary is useful when ZapJS needs worker isolation or binary replacement. It stays inside framework-owned lifecycle management for ordinary deployments.
Streaming is not advertised until credit-based stream backpressure is implemented and tested. The current contract deliberately names only the behavior the transport already proves.
Most application work should stay in direct Rust calls inside the managed function artifact unless a measured isolation or replacement need justifies a worker boundary.
author: ZapJS

title: Performance claims need production evidence
excerpt: ZapJS optimizes the full request path, but speed claims require matched workloads and measured artifacts.
paragraphs: The framework architecture starts by removing work before optimizing what remains. ZapJS starts with prerendering, explicit cache policy, smaller browser bundles and waterfall removal; streaming backpressure is not a public claim until the final pipeline proves it.

Rust is used where profiling shows substantial CPU work, lifecycle control, artifact packaging or runtime isolation benefits. A fast router or isolated transport measurement is not page latency evidence.

Production claims require equivalent behavior, pinned framework versions, cold and warm measurements, memory, CPU, throughput, client JavaScript transfer, browser-visible rendering and error rates under a stated load target.
Until those measurements exist for the Rust-owned vertical slice, the website should present architecture and verification status rather than universal speedups.
author: ZapJS
